power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Study 1 was recruited from CloudResearch in two waves, each advertised as a 17.5minute study and run under one protocol, apart from two sentences of the No Facts prompt (SI S6.2; raw N = 3,988; 2,585 in Sample 1a and 1,403 in Sample 1b). The first wave (Sample 1a) was the original preregistered launch. Our preregistered allocation in Sample 1a was n = 200 per active condition and n = 400 in the Baseline treatment (more in the Baseline treatment to increase between-group precision). The preregistration listed ten conditions; two open-access model-comparison arms (Llama 3 70B and Llama 2 13B), together with an exploratory GPT-3.5 arm, were run only as a Sample 1a pilot (n = 173 after screening) and are excluded from all analyses (Figure S1). After Sample 1a closed, the rate at which open-ended responses were classified as a conspiracy belief was lower than our preregistration assumed, so we ran a second wave (Sample 1b). Sample 1b used weighted randomization that, after pooling across waves, brought each of the eight remaining conditions close to its target sample size; sample size was indexed to a power calculation on Sample 1a effect sizes, which found that n = 150 per active arm and n = 350 in the Baseline treatment gave 80% power to detect a halving of treatment efficacy relative to the Baseline treatment. The exclusions, applied in order, were: failed CAPTCHA (n = 8), accessed the survey on a mobile device (n = 20), did not reach or failed the embedded attention check (n = 297), did not reach the AI treatment (n = 163), assigned to the pilot model-comparison arms (n = 173), did not articulate a conspiracy belief (n = 1,828), pretreatment belief below 50/100 (n = 96), missing post-treatment belief (attrition; n = 38), and cross-wave duplicates dropped at the participant ID level (n = 75). The full cascade is shown in Figure S1. The final analytic sample was N = 1,290 (Sample 1a: 806; Sample 1b: 484). Percondition ns after pooling were Baseline treatment = 333, Abstracted Summary = 164, Belief-First Rating = 137, Concise = 137, Adversarial = 131, No Facts = 129, Overt = 132, Just-the-Facts = 127.
table.effect_size_metric_other: halving of treatment efficacy relative to the Baseline treatment

table.text: Five Study 1 conditions were designed as targeted ablations of the Baseline treatment, and two altered the measurement procedure (Table 1). We compared the post-treatment belief score of each condition against the Baseline treatment while controlling for pre-treatment belief, and we report contrasts as differences in belief reduction, so that positive values indicate a larger reduction than in the Baseline treatment. In addition to the preregistered linear regressions, we also conducted complementary post hoc Bayesian regressions (Figure 1A). Given that many of the results are nulls, in the main text we focus on the Bayesian analyses as they quantify evidence for the null-difference interpretation rather than merely failure to reject it (full frequentist statistics for all contrasts are provided in Supplemental Tables S6 and S8, and are qualitatively equivalent). These contrasts could detect only large differences: each null contrast had 80% power for a difference of about 6-7 points, that is, 53-63% of the Baseline effect.

table.text: Participants in Study 2 likewise entered with strong endorsement of their focal conspiracy theories (pretreatment M = 80.7). In the Baseline treatment, belief decreased from 80.5 to 65.9, a mean reduction of 14.6 points, replicating Study 1, whereas the Control condition showed only a 1.4-point mean reduction (posterior mean difference from the Baseline treatment = -13.11, 95% CrI [-16.52, -9.71], BF10 > 1,000; Baseline treatment vs. Control d ppc = 0.88, 95% CI [0.69, 1.07], p < .001; Figure 1B); the Baseline effect is therefore not attributable to regression to the mean. Among Baseline-treatment participants who began above the scale midpoint, 23.1% (75 of 324) ended below it, compared with 1.5% (3 of 197) in Control (Fisher's exact p < .001; Supplemental Table S9). Study 2 then asked whether the dialogic format itself was critical. As in Study 1, each condition was compared with the Baseline treatment, controlling for pretreatment belief, with the Baseline treatment as the reference group (Figure 1B; Table S8). The Single Message produced a large reduction relative to Control (posterior mean difference = 10.28, 95% CrI [6.93, 13.65], BF10 > 1,000; Single Message vs. Control d ppc = 0.69, 95% CI [0.53, 0.87], p < .001), with a raw decrease of 11.76 points and 16.8% of participants who began above the midpoint ending below it. Compared with the Baseline treatment, the Single Message reduced belief by slightly less (posterior mean difference = -2.82, 95% CrI [-5.71, 0.06], BF01 = 2.1; HC3 b = 2.87 on the post-treatment belief scale, 95% CI [-0.36, 6.10], p = .081; d ppc = -0.19, 95% CI [-0.41, 0.02]), retaining an estimated 79% of the Baseline effect (95% CrI [58%, 101%]); this contrast had 80% power to detect a difference of about 4.6 points (35% of the Baseline effect). Thus, even when the treatment was reduced to a single tailored AI responsewith no iterative give-and-take, no ongoing rapport-building, and no dynamic responding -it produced a large reduction in conspiracy belief. Multi-turn dialogue is therefore not necessary to obtain a large effect, although it may confer some additional benefit beyond the static message.
table.header: Which Ingredients of the Treatment Were Necessary?

table.text: Each Study 1 null contrast could detect only large differences: with 80% power, 5.8-6.8 points, or 53-63% of the Baseline treatment's 10.88-point reduction; power to detect a halving of the effect (5.44 points) was .61 to .75. Table S7 reports what the six variants that did not differ from Baseline rule out. All six pass a one-sided non-inferiority test against a half-effect margin (Holm-adjusted p < .05), and the posterior probability that each retains at least half the Baseline effect is ≥ .97. Only for Overt does the 95% interval include a loss of more than half the effect. Two-sided equivalence tests at the same margin fail only for Concise (p = .13) and Abstracted Summary (p = .07), whose estimates lie above Baseline. On average the six variants differ from Baseline by 0.62 points (HC3 95% CI [-2.07, 3.31]). The half-effect margin is lenient, and because Study 1 has no untreated control, the shares are relative to pre-post change, which includes roughly 1.4-1.5 points of untreated drift (Study 2 Control).

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: LLM Persuasion Experiment (Extension #1 of Costello et al. 2024)
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: This study examines how various factors impact the ability of large language models to reduce belief in conspiracies, including (1) different AI model prompts, (2) different AI models (including older versions and non-OpenAI models), (3) changes to the pre- and post-treatment measurement materials, (4) changes to AI summarization of conspiracy beliefs, and (5) varying instructions for the human research subjects.
table.design_dependent_variables: Post-treatment belief in participants' focal conspiracy (controlling for pre-treatment belief) will be the key dependent variable.
table.study_design_overview:
Participants will enter either a baseline condition or one of 9 experimental conditions. No conditions will be crossed. 

Prompt Variations:

Condition 1: Instructing GPT-4 Turbo to persuade without using reason-based strategies. 

Condition 2: Instructing GPT-4 Turbo to provide accurate information about the conspiracy belief, but not otherwise attempt to persuade the participant.

Condition 3: Curtailing the length of GPT-4's responses

Model Comparisons:

Condition 4: Using LLama 3 70B rather than GPT-4 Turbo

Condition 5: LLama 2 13b rather than GPT-4 Turbo 

Pre- and Post-Treatment Measures:

Condition 6: Asking participants to indicate their level of belief in the chosen conspiracy before asking them to provide evidence supporting their belief. 

AI Summarization Changes:

Condition 7: When the AI is tasked with summarizing participants' conspiracy beliefs – so as to provide a person-specific measurement occasion – it will exclude any specific evidence from the summary. 

Instructions for Human Subjects:

Condition 8: Telling participants that the AI will be trying to persuade them prior to the dialogues. 

Condition 9: Telling participants that they will be debating with the AI, which is trying to persuade them against their conspiracy belief, prior to the dialogues.
table.statistical_tests: We will conduct a series of linear regression analyses comparing each experimental condition against the baseline condition using the following model: Post-treatment belief ~ [Dummy coded variable for baseline vs. condition] + pre-treatment belief). Statistical inference will be drawn using two-tailed t-tests for the Condition coefficient. We will also compare changes in model fit (i.e., with the addition of the Condition dummy-coded variables into the model) using R-squared values and Bayesian Information Criterion. The alpha level for the addition of the dummy-coded variables into the model will be set at 0.05.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Participants who provide an initial belief rating below 50% certainty for their focal conspiracy theory will be excluded.
Participants who do not report believing in a conspiracy theory will be excluded (using the procedures in Costello et al. [2024]). 
Participants who do not pass the initial writing quality screener will be excluded.
Participants who fail an attention check prior to treatment will be excluded.
table.sample_size:
Each condition will have a target sample size of 200 participants, except for the baseline condition which will aim for 400 participants to provide a comprehensive comparison group.
Total planned sample size is thus 2,200 participants.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report:
Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

live_data_statements: Other conditions hold that content constant while varying how the AI or the interaction is framed to participants: Overt, in which participants are told of the AI's persuasive goal, and Adversarial, in which the exchange is framed as a debate.
Study 2 also included a Control condition wherein participants completed an AI conversation on a topic unrelated to conspiracy beliefs.

To reduce the chance that results would depend on any one arbitrary control topic, control participants were randomly assigned to one of three unrelated conversation topics (experiences with the American medical system, views about firefighters, or cats versus dogs as companions).

Study 1 was recruited from CloudResearch in two waves, each advertised as a 17.5minute study and run under one protocol, apart from two sentences of the No Facts prompt (SI S6.2; raw N = 3,988; 2,585 in Sample 1a and 1,403 in Sample 1b).

Study 2 was recruited from CloudResearch in a single wave under the same intake protocol as Study 1 (raw N = 2,082); the preregistered target was 400 conspiracy believers in each treatment arm and 200 in Control (the sensitivity of the achieved sample is reported with the Study 2 results).
Participants were U.S. adults recruited through CloudResearch Connect who completed the study in English; all descriptive statistics refer to the final analytic samples.
In Study 1, conspiracy-believing participants were more Republicanleaning (party preference d = 0.35; 39% vs.
80.5; difference = 2.03, 95% CI [-0.95, 5.01], p = .18), and participants were no more likely to flag the shorter statement as an inaccurate summary of their belief (3.6% vs.

Participants are the Study 1 analytic sample excluding No Facts, restricted to the 1,058 with a non-empty explanation and cached codes (codes exist for 1,061 of 1,161 eligible participants; three blank responses were excluded).
Study 1 ran in two waves from the same participant pool under one protocol, apart from two sentences of the No Facts prompt (Samples 1a and 1b; §S6.2).
After giving consent, participants completed a CAPTCHA; those who failed it or opened the survey on a mobile device were screened out ( §S2.1).
Participants were then randomly assigned to a condition (Table S1; a ninth, alternative-model arm in Sample 1a is excluded, §S2.1).
In the Abstracted Summary condition, the summarization prompt also told the AI not to mention any specific evidence the participant had given ( §S1.3.1).
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions, all run with GPT-5.2 (gpt-5.2-2025-12-11).
In Control, participants had a conversation of comparable format on one of three unrelated topics, assigned at random: the American medical system, firefighters, or cats versus dogs.

Participants were excluded if they (a) failed the attention check (one item in Study 1, two in Study 2; §S1.3.5), (b) failed the writing screener ( §S1.3.3), which ran inside the survey before the experiment and so has no step in Figures S1-S2, (c) did not articulate a conspiracy belief according to the classifier ( §S1.3.2), or (d) rated their pretreatment belief below 50.

Another 75 retained records are a participant's second submission whose first had been excluded earlier in the cascade (58 of these participants had already talked with the AI in the alternative-model arm or the non-conspiracy branch).

The analysis in the main text (Figure 3C) uses Study 1 of Costello et al. (2024), whose participants completed the six-item AOT subscale (1-6, all items reverse-scored; α = .91, M = 4.11, SD = 1.05) at a follow-up a median of 12.0 days after the experiment (IQR 11.8-12.3).

The bracketed fields were filled with the Table S31 definitions, the attribute being coded, the question the participant had answered, and whether their belief had fallen ("succeeded") or not ("failed"); the condition was not given.

text.text: Personalized dialogues with AI substantially reduce conspiracy beliefs.
To identify why, we conducted two experiments with U.S. adults recruited online (total N = 2,193) that removed possible causes one at a time.

The debunking effect was robust to disclosing the AI's persuasive goal, framing the exchange as a debate, instructing the AI to inform rather than persuade, halving its response length, altering how beliefs were measured, and replacing the dialogue with a single tailored message.
Only instructing the AI to persuade without factual evidence and arguments substantially reduced the debunking effect.
Content analyses of the AI's output and participants' own accounts linked larger reductions in conspiracy beliefs to factual argumentation rather than rapport, storytelling, or appeals to empathy.
AI dialogues appear to reduce conspiracy beliefs primarily by supplying relevant, well-reasoned counterevidence.
Our results suggest that humans might be similarly effective if they could supply comparable evidence.

Conspiracy theories -explanations of important events as secret, malevolent plots by powerful actors -are widespread and can have serious consequences for public health, democratic legitimacy, extremism, and scientific progress (Ecker et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Conspiracy theories -explanations of important events as secret, malevolent plots by powerful actors -are widespread and can have serious consequences for public health, democratic legitimacy, extremism, and scientific progress <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Ecker et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although some conspiracies are real, many popular conspiracy beliefs are clearly contradicted by evidence but are nonetheless hard to correct.

In meta-analyses, corrections of conspiracy theories and related misinformation have reliable but typically modest effects that often shrink or vanish for highly committed believers or ideologically resonant claims (Albarracin & Shavitt, 2018; Chan & Albarracín, 2023; Walter et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In meta-analyses, corrections of conspiracy theories and related misinformation have reliable but typically modest effects that often shrink or vanish for highly committed believers or ideologically resonant claims <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Albarracin & Shavitt, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Chan & Albarracín, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Walter et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Lay and academic accounts have therefore often assumed that no brief intervention, least of all one that simply presents counterevidence, can durably move such beliefs (Lewandowsky et al., 2013; O'Mahony et al., 2023; Sunstein & Vermeule, 2009), which are seen as sustained by motivated reasoning, distrust of official sources, and selfsealing explanation (Biddlestone et al., 2021; Dagnall et al., 2015; Douglas et al., 2024) or as socially adaptive commitments or group-signaling rationalizations rather than attempts to track truth (Mercier, 2020; Williams, 2023).
text.formatted: Lay and academic accounts have therefore often assumed that no brief intervention, least of all one that simply presents counterevidence, can durably move such beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lewandowsky et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">O'Mahony et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Sunstein & Vermeule, 2009)</ref>, which are seen as sustained by motivated reasoning, distrust of official sources, and selfsealing explanation <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Biddlestone et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Dagnall et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Douglas et al., 2024)</ref> or as socially adaptive commitments or group-signaling rationalizations rather than attempts to track truth <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Mercier, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Williams, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, recent evidence indicates that personalized dialogues with AI models can meaningfully reduce conspiracy beliefs (Costello et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, recent evidence indicates that personalized dialogues with AI models can meaningfully reduce conspiracy beliefs <ref type="bibr">(Costello et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In these studies, a substantial fraction of believers revised their beliefs after sustained, belief-relevant counterargumentation, with unusually large effects (ds of 0.79 and 1.15).
This finding may complicate, or even run counter to, portraits of conspiracy believers as insensitive to evidence because they are motivated by needs other than accuracy.
What, exactly, underpins the AI's outsized effect?
One account is content-based.
In classical reasoning and Bayesian accounts of belief updating, sufficiently diagnostic counterevidence should induce deliberation and subsequent belief revision (Pennycook, 2023).
text.formatted: In classical reasoning and Bayesian accounts of belief updating, sufficiently diagnostic counterevidence should induce deliberation and subsequent belief revision <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Pennycook, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As such, the treatment would succeed by presenting relevant counterevidence, reasoning, and alternative explanations that directly address participants' stated reasons for believing.

Generative AI may be distinctive in delivering expert-level knowledge across remarkably broad domains (Farrell et al., 2025; Singhal et al., 2025), whereas any human debunker, however well informed, commands only a small fraction of the counterevidence relevant to the conspiracies participants might name and so cannot reliably tailor arguments to each believer's claims and reasoning (Costello, 2025; Williams, 2026); the AI's advantage would lie in its informational facility.
text.formatted: Generative AI may be distinctive in delivering expert-level knowledge across remarkably broad domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Farrell et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Singhal et al., 2025)</ref>, whereas any human debunker, however well informed, commands only a small fraction of the counterevidence relevant to the conspiracies participants might name and so cannot reliably tailor arguments to each believer's claims and reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Costello, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Williams, 2026)</ref>; the AI's advantage would lie in its informational facility.

text.text: Another class of accounts is source-based: participants defer to the AI because of what they think it is.

AI systems may be seen as more objective, neutral, accurate, or less politically motivated than human interlocutors, consistent with work on source credibility and "machine heuristic" effects (Hovland & Weiss, 1951; Pornpitakpan, 2004; Sundar & Kim, 2019).
text.formatted: AI systems may be seen as more objective, neutral, accurate, or less politically motivated than human interlocutors, consistent with work on source credibility and "machine heuristic" effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Hovland & Weiss, 1951;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Pornpitakpan, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Sundar & Kim, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: People sometimes prefer algorithmic to human judgment ("algorithm appreciation"; Logg et al., 2019), although "algorithm aversion," harsher judgment of algorithms' mistakes than of humans', is also well documented (Dietvorst et al., 2015).
text.formatted: People sometimes prefer algorithmic to human judgment ("algorithm appreciation"; <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Logg et al., 2019)</ref>, although "algorithm aversion," harsher judgment of algorithms' mistakes than of humans', is also well documented <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dietvorst et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Because participants in the original paradigm were told they would be talking to a neutral AI system (Costello et al., 2024), belief reductions may reflect deference to an apparently impartial, epistemically privileged source rather than (or in concert with) the content of the arguments (Glickman & Sharot, 2024).
text.formatted: Because participants in the original paradigm were told they would be talking to a neutral AI system <ref type="bibr">(Costello et al., 2024)</ref>, belief reductions may reflect deference to an apparently impartial, epistemically privileged source rather than (or in concert with) the content of the arguments <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Glickman & Sharot, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A third class of accounts is interaction-based: the treatment's persuasive force depends on the dialogic, human-AI "chatbot" format.

Conversations are a potent means of arbitrating between truth and falsehood (Mercier, 2016), and human-AI conversations are unusually personalized, judgment-free, socially warm, and non-adversarial, which may reduce defensiveness, increase engagement, or make participants feel understood (Sherman & Cohen, 2006).
text.formatted: Conversations are a potent means of arbitrating between truth and falsehood <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Mercier, 2016)</ref>, and human-AI conversations are unusually personalized, judgment-free, socially warm, and non-adversarial, which may reduce defensiveness, increase engagement, or make participants feel understood <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Sherman & Cohen, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Sustained, respectful dialogue has also been argued to be central to the unusually durable attitude change produced by deep canvassing (Kalla & Broockman, 2020) and motivational interviewing (Miller & Rollnick, 2013).
text.formatted: Sustained, respectful dialogue has also been argued to be central to the unusually durable attitude change produced by deep canvassing <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kalla & Broockman, 2020)</ref> and motivational interviewing <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Miller & Rollnick, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Dialogic AI's rhetorical fluency, long and informationally dense responses, and repeated back-and-forth opportunities to wear down objections could also drive the effect.
A final possibility is deflationary: the effect may partly reflect how belief was measured.
In the original paradigm, participants named a conspiracy they believed and why, elaborated on their evidence, and only then rated their belief in an AI-generated restatement of their account.

Because elaborating on a belief can itself prompt reflection or expose gaps in understanding (Fox et al., 2011; Sloman & Vives, 2022), the baseline rating, and the change measured from it, may depend on when elaboration occurs.
text.formatted: Because elaborating on a belief can itself prompt reflection or expose gaps in understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Fox et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Sloman & Vives, 2022)</ref>, the baseline rating, and the change measured from it, may depend on when elaboration occurs.

text.text: And because the rated statement often incorporates the evidence participants cited, apparent change could reflect a narrow concession that those particular reasons were wrong, even if participants still hold the conspiracy to be true.
To address these questions, we systematically manipulated core elements that relate to each underlying possible causal factor (or set of factors).
Study 1 begins with a baseline treatment that closely replicates the original AI dialogue treatment from Costello et al. (2024), then varies its features one at a time (Table 1).
text.formatted: Study 1 begins with a baseline treatment that closely replicates the original AI dialogue treatment from <ref type="bibr">Costello et al. (2024)</ref>, then varies its features one at a time (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Some conditions target the content of the AI's response: No Facts, in which the model is instructed to persuade without using rational argumentation or evidence; Just-the-Facts, in which the model is prompted to inform rather than persuade; and Concise, in which the model produces substantially shorter responses.

Other conditions hold that content constant while varying how the AI or the interaction is framed to participants: Overt, in which participants are told of the AI's persuasive goal, and Adversarial, in which the exchange is framed as a debate.
Two additional variations change the order of the conspiracy measurement and the specificity of the AI-generated belief summary.

Each content or framing condition is therefore a targeted ablation: attenuated belief change relative to the Baseline treatment implicates the removed ingredient, whereas an unchanged effect shows that it was not necessary.

Study 2 compares the Baseline treatment with (i) a single AI-generated message, to probe the importance of the dialogue, and (ii) a Control dialogue about an irrelevant topic, to rule out regression to the mean.

We also analyze moderators (Study 2) and the content of the AI's responses (both studies) post hoc.  & S2) A live, multi-turn dialogue in which the AI counters the participant's belief with reasons and evidence, replicating what led them to find that theory compelling, including any evidence, events, sources of information, or personal experiences they saw as supportive.

text.text: Those responses were then passed to a live GPT-4-family model, which restated the participant's focal belief as a standardized psychometric item.
Participants rated their confidence in that statement on a 0-100 scale (0 = Definitely false,50 = Uncertain,100 = Definitely true).
This served as the pre-treatment belief measure.
(In the Belief-First Rating condition of Study 1, the statement was generated from the first response alone and rated before the elaboration prompt.)

To ensure that the paradigm targeted genuine conspiracy beliefs, participants' open-ended responses were also classified using the large language model (LLM)-assisted conspiracy-classification procedure described in Costello et al. (2024), which has shown strong convergence with human judgment (Gwet's AC1 = .80 [.72, .89]); Study 2 used gpt-4o with a more inclusive classification prompt (Supplemental Materials [SI] S1.3.2) and an altered restatement prompt.

(2024)</ref>, which has shown strong convergence with human judgment (Gwet's AC1 = .80 [.72, .89]); Study 2 used gpt-4o with a more inclusive classification prompt (Supplemental Materials [SI] S1.3.2) and an altered restatement prompt.

text.text: Articulating a conspiracy belief and rating the focal statement at or above the scale midpoint were preregistered analytic eligibility criteria applied to these pretreatment measures.
Participants who failed attention checks or the writing-quality screener (both also preregistered), submitted duplicate responses, or used mobile devices were also excluded (SI S2.1).

To prevent and detect automated or AI-generated responses, both studies began with a CAPTCHA, and the writing-quality screener was scored by an LLM instructed to flag incoherent, low-effort, or apparently AI-written answers (SI S1.3.3).
Immediately before the treatment, participants saw condition-specific instructions.

Verbatim system-prompt and participant-facing instructions for every condition are reproduced in Supplemental Table S1; pre/post measurement items and attention checks are listed in SI S1.3, and key pretreatment moderator items are quoted under Measures below.
text.formatted: Verbatim system-prompt and participant-facing instructions for every condition are reproduced in Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>; pre/post measurement items and attention checks are listed in SI S1.3, and key pretreatment moderator items are quoted under Measures below.

text.text: In all active conditions, AI responses were generated live via API call to GPT-4 (Study 1) or GPT-5.2 (Study 2) rather than selected from a fixed bank of prewritten messages.
Study 2 also included a Control condition wherein participants completed an AI conversation on a topic unrelated to conspiracy beliefs.

To reduce the chance that results would depend on any one arbitrary control topic, control participants were randomly assigned to one of three unrelated conversation topics (experiences with the American medical system, views about firefighters, or cats versus dogs as companions).
After the conversation with the AI, participants again rated belief in the focal conspiracy statement, providing the primary outcome measure.
They then completed posttreatment questions; in Study 1, these included a brief open-ended explanation of why they did or did not find the AI's comments persuasive.

Study 1 was recruited from CloudResearch in two waves, each advertised as a 17.5minute study and run under one protocol, apart from two sentences of the No Facts prompt (SI S6.2; raw N = 3,988; 2,585 in Sample 1a and 1,403 in Sample 1b).
The first wave (Sample 1a) was the original preregistered launch.
Our preregistered allocation in Sample 1a was n = 200 per active condition and n = 400 in the Baseline treatment (more in the Baseline treatment to increase between-group precision).

The preregistration listed ten conditions; two open-access model-comparison arms (Llama 3 70B and Llama 2 13B), together with an exploratory GPT-3.5 arm, were run only as a Sample 1a pilot (n = 173 after screening) and are excluded from all analyses (Figure S1).

text.text: After Sample 1a closed, the rate at which open-ended responses were classified as a conspiracy belief was lower than our preregistration assumed, so we ran a second wave (Sample 1b).

Sample 1b used weighted randomization that, after pooling across waves, brought each of the eight remaining conditions close to its target sample size; sample size was indexed to a power calculation on Sample 1a effect sizes, which found that n = 150 per active arm and n = 350 in the Baseline treatment gave 80% power to detect a halving of treatment efficacy relative to the Baseline treatment.

The exclusions, applied in order, were: failed CAPTCHA (n = 8), accessed the survey on a mobile device (n = 20), did not reach or failed the embedded attention check (n = 297), did not reach the AI treatment (n = 163), assigned to the pilot model-comparison arms (n = 173), did not articulate a conspiracy belief (n = 1,828), pretreatment belief below 50/100 (n = 96), missing post-treatment belief (attrition; n = 38), and cross-wave duplicates dropped at the participant ID level (n = 75).
The full cascade is shown in Figure S1.

text.text: The final analytic sample was N = 1,290 (Sample 1a: 806; Sample 1b: 484).
Percondition ns after pooling were Baseline treatment = 333, Abstracted Summary = 164, Belief-First Rating = 137, Concise = 137, Adversarial = 131, No Facts = 129, Overt = 132, Just-the-Facts = 127.

Study 2 was recruited from CloudResearch in a single wave under the same intake protocol as Study 1 (raw N = 2,082); the preregistered target was 400 conspiracy believers in each treatment arm and 200 in Control (the sensitivity of the achieved sample is reported with the Study 2 results).

The exclusions, applied in order, were: mobile use at outset (n = 483); did not reach condition assignment (n = 136); not classified as a conspiracy belief by the LLM classifier (n = 296); pre-treatment belief below 50 (n = 126); failed at least one of two attention checks (n = 24); flagged the AI-generated summary of their belief as inaccurate (n = 88); and missing post-treatment belief (attrition; n = 26).
The final analytic sample was N = 903.
Percondition ns were Single Message = 364, Baseline treatment = 336, and Control = 203 (Cats / Dogs = 58; Firefighters = 75; Medical system = 70).
The full cascade is shown in Figure S2.

text.text: Participants were U.S. adults recruited through CloudResearch Connect who completed the study in English; all descriptive statistics refer to the final analytic samples.

In Study 1 (N = 1,290), mean age was 36.4 years (SD = 10.9); 54.9% identified as female, 43.4% as male, and 1.7% as nonbinary or another gender (or preferred not to say); 54.7% held a bachelor's degree or higher; 39.3% identified as Democrats, 29.4% as Independents, and 23.4% as Republicans; and 25.2% were Protestant and 13.6% Roman Catholic.

Study 2 (N = 903) was sampled to balance partisanship (47.0% Democrat, 46.5% Republican); mean age was 40.9 years (SD = 13.8), 56.1% identified as female, 41.9% as male, and 2.0% as nonbinary or another gender (or preferred not to say), 57.0% held a bachelor's degree or higher, and 32.0% were Protestant and 18.7% Roman Catholic.

Alongside the first rating, participants answered "Did the AI accurately summarize your perspective?"

(social embeddedness; a single 0-100 slider labeled No, none of them; Yes, 1-2 of them; Yes, all of them) and rated four statements on a 5-point scale (Strongly disagree, Somewhat disagree, Neither agree nor disagree, Somewhat agree, Strongly agree).
"I have heard many arguments against this belief before" and "I have discussed this belief with people who disagreed with me" were averaged as prior exposure to counterarguments (r = .45, α = .62).

text.text: Three post hoc content-coding schemes were applied by large language models at temperature 0 (SI S6.1, S7.1-S7.2, S9.1).

First, to characterize the AI's persuasive approach, each conversation was rated on 16 persuasion strategies (e.g., presenting conflicting evidence, offering alternative explanations, building rapport, telling stories, citing credible sources).

The list comes from the analysis code of Costello et al. (2024), where candidate strategies had been generated by repeatedly asking  Turbo what strategies it would use to dissuade someone from a conspiracy belief and retaining the recurring ones.

text.text: GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) rated each of the AI's three messages in each conversation on each strategy (none, low, moderate, high), one call per strategy per conversation; we analyze the ratings of the first message.
Second, to characterize the content of the AI's messages at a finer grain, GPT-4.1 first extracted each specific factual claim in each AI message (excluding opinions, advice, and general rhetoric).

Each distinct claim was then classified into one of six categories (specific empirical, inferentiallogical, meta-epistemic, moral/political, minimal/non-adjudicative, or general/underspecified) by Gemini 3 Flash.
The categories were developed inductively.

Third, to code participants' own explanations of why the AI was or was not persuasive, we developed 15 attributes (six positive, e.g., facts and logic, tailoring to the participant's claims; nine negative, e.g., perceived bias, lack of depth) by combining human review of the responses with candidate categories generated by an AI model given the same responses into a single taxonomy.
GPT-4o judged each attribute present or absent in each response.

Taken together, these results support evidence-based argumentation as a key driver of the AI's effect on conspiracy belief, while providing evidence against each of the other candidate explanations being necessary for a large effect.

text.text: Compared with the Baseline treatment, the Single Message reduced belief by slightly less (posterior mean difference = -2.82, 95% CrI [-5.71, 0.06], BF01 = 2.1; HC3 b = 2.87 on the post-treatment belief scale, 95% CI [-0.36, 6.10], p = .081; d ppc = -0.19, 95% CI [-0.41, 0.02]), retaining an estimated 79% of the Baseline effect (95% CrI [58%, 101%]); this contrast had 80% power to detect a difference of about 4.6 points (35% of the Baseline effect).

Thus, even when the treatment was reduced to a single tailored AI responsewith no iterative give-and-take, no ongoing rapport-building, and no dynamic responding -it produced a large reduction in conspiracy belief.
Multi-turn dialogue is therefore not necessary to obtain a large effect, although it may confer some additional benefit beyond the static message.
Attrition in Study 2 differed by condition, χ²(2, N = 929) = 12.22, p = .002: Baseline treatment 5.08% (18/354), Single Message 0.82% (3/367), and Control 2.40% (5/208).

To assess sensitivity to this differential attrition, we followed Costello et al. (2024) and conducted post hoc baseline-carried-forward-imputation analyses in which the 26 participants who dropped out after beginning the chat were assigned a post-treatment belief equal to their pre-treatment belief (i.e., a treatment effect of zero) and added to the analytic sample (N = 929).

text.text: We found a positive interaction between trust in AI and treatment (posterior mean = 2.13 points per trust scale point, 95% CrI [1.09, 3.16], BF10 > 30; HC3 b = 2.13, 95% CI [1.29, 2.98], p < .001; Figure 3A), which did not differ detectably across the three experiments (p = .317).

text.text: Substantively, however, the treatment remained highly effective even among participants with low trust in AI (e.g., 10.7 belief points at 1 SD below mean AI trust, 95% CrI [8.3, 13.1]).
Greater trust in AI may modestly facilitate the treatment but is not necessary for it.
A second possibility is that the social context in which a belief is held bounds the treatment's efficacy, such that beliefs reinforced by one's social network do not respond to correction.

78.7%, p = .822), which makes that reading less likely.

In Study 2, we found no significant moderation of the Baseline treatment effect by pretreatment belief (b = -0.86 points per SD, 95% CI [-3.77, 2.04], p = .559), education (b = -2.60, 95% CI [-5.27, 0.07], p = .056), religiosity (b = -0.94, 95% CI [-3.92, 2.04], p = .537), age (b = -0.39, 95% CI [-3.25, 2.47], p = .790), or party identification (Republicans vs.

To better understand how the AI reduced conspiracy beliefs -and why the No Facts condition in particular was much less effective -we conducted two complementary post hoc content analyses.
We first characterize the dialogues at the level of broad persuasive strategies (Study 1), then drill down to the level of individual claims (Studies 1 and 2).
The coding procedures are described in the Method.

We focused on the four Study 1 conditions that most directly manipulated the AI's conversational behavior (Baseline treatment, Just-the-Facts, No Facts, Concise), analyzed as randomized within the analytic sample (n = 309, 111, 116, and 123, respectively; N = 659).

GPT-4o rated the AI's first message in each conversation on 16 candidate persuasion strategies (four-level ordinal scale: none / low / moderate / high; definitions of all 16 strategies in Supplemental Table S19).

text.text: Because many strategies were conceptually overlapping, we summarized them using a polychoric-correlation principal component analysis (PCA) with varimax rotation.

Strategy labels still leave open a substantive question: What did "facts and evidence" actually consist of?

To answer this question, we passed each saved AI message to GPT-4.1 and had it extract the specific factual claims in that message (the extraction prompt excluded opinions, advice, and general rhetoric).

We then deduplicated the claim texts and coded them with Gemini 3 Flash using a codebook with six top-level categories: specific empirical claims, inferential-logical claims, meta-epistemic claims, moral/political evaluation claims, minimal / non-adjudicative claims, and general or underspecified claims (see Table 2 for examples; the codebook is in SI Section S7.2, Table S23, with subtypes in S7.7).

The pipeline yielded 30,662 claim instances (30,314 distinct claim texts) in Study 1 and 27,535 claim instances (27,352 distinct claim texts) in Study 2.

Pooling across all Study 1 conditions, the distribution of distinct claims was 47.4% specific empirical, 24.1% minimal / non-adjudicative, 15.2% general/underspecified, 6.2% moral/political, 4.1% inferential-logical, and 2.9% meta-epistemic.

Together with the experimental contrasts, this indicates that the full amount of information the Baseline AI provided is not required for a comparable effect.

As a final post hoc analysis, we examined the free-text responses collected at the end of Study 1 (Study 2 did not include these items).

Participants whose post-treatment rating was lower than their pre-treatment rating were asked what about the AI's comments they found persuasive (n = 584 with coded responses), and those whose rating was unchanged or higher were asked why they found the comments unpersuasive (n = 474; see Measures).

As described in the Method, GPT-4o coded each response for the presence or absence of each of 15 attributes covering positive themes (e.g., factual content, tailored argument, expertise, emotional synchrony) and criticisms (e.g., perceived bias, repetitiveness, off-topic drift, obsequiousness; full codebook in Table S31).

text.text: Persuaded participants overwhelmingly cited the AI's provision of tailored facts, evidence, and logic, with far fewer mentioning its trustworthiness or expertise (Figure 6).

text.text: These analyses thus further emphasize the importance of evidence and reasoning for belief updating, while also being consistent with our observation that trust in AI moderates the treatment effect to some extent.

Previous work has established that conversations with generative AI can substantially reduce belief in conspiracies (Costello et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Previous work has established that conversations with generative AI can substantially reduce belief in conspiracies <ref type="bibr">(Costello et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Here we probed a set of theoretical and methodological claims about why this effect occurs.

In Study 1, six of seven variationsremoving the AI's apparent neutrality, its non-adversarial framing, its persuasive intent, and roughly half of its verbosity, and altering two features of the measurement procedure -left the effect intact; only instructing the AI to persuade without evidence, counterargument, or reasoning sharply weakened it.

In analyses of what the AI said, belief change tracked its reliance on evidence and reasoned rebuttal, not rapport-building, storytelling, or appeals to empathy, and persuaded participants most often cited its factual arguments.
We thus find strong evidence that an evidence-rich argumentative package featuring facts is a necessary and central mechanism of the effect.
In Study 2, a single tailored message retained an estimated 79% of the full dialogue's effect and far exceeded an unrelated-topic control dialogue, in which belief did not move.
Dialogue may confer some additional benefit, but much of the effect can be achieved with a single message tailored to the specific belief.

Our data also argue against several other candidate features being necessary for a large debunking effect: the AI's rhetorical abilities (arranging words persuasively with substantive content held fixed), its ability to converse, its rapport and social warmth, the machine heuristic or algorithm aversion, measurement error, regression to the mean, and information overload.

That said, our studies could detect only large differences between treatment arms (about half to twothirds of the Baseline effect in Study 1 and about one third in Study 2), and we did not experimentally increase these elements or manipulate them in combination.
Individual features, including multi-turn dialogue and trust in AI, may therefore contribute to the effect but to a smaller degree.
Identifying the potentiating and inhibitory features of AI-based argumentation is a fruitful direction for future research (Jones & Bergen, 2024).
text.formatted: Identifying the potentiating and inhibitory features of AI-based argumentation is a fruitful direction for future research <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Jones & Bergen, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, what we do show is that none of these elements are necessary for a large effect.
Nor do they themselves evidently produce large effects.
Recent external findings converge with this picture.

First, in the same paradigm, believing one was talking to a human expert rather than an AI produced comparable belief reductions (Boissin et al., 2025), so the effect does not rely on deference to AI as a source.
text.formatted: First, in the same paradigm, believing one was talking to a human expert rather than an AI produced comparable belief reductions <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Boissin et al., 2025)</ref>, so the effect does not rely on deference to AI as a source.

text.text: Second, the effect persisted without substantive change at a 2-month follow-up (Costello et al., 2024), suggesting that the updating is not a fleeting demand artifact.
text.formatted: Second, the effect persisted without substantive change at a 2-month follow-up <ref type="bibr">(Costello et al., 2024)</ref>, suggesting that the updating is not a fleeting demand artifact.

text.text: Third, research in other domains has found support for the role of facts and evidence in AI-mediated belief updating. Lin et al. (2025) found that depriving AI canvassers of factual claims dramatically reduced their persuasiveness in the 2025 Canadian national and Polish presidential elections, and Hackenburg et al. (2025) found that instructing an AI to persuade with large quantities of facts and evidence was the most effective strategy on UK political issues.
text.formatted: Third, research in other domains has found support for the role of facts and evidence in AI-mediated belief updating. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Lin et al. (2025)</ref> found that depriving AI canvassers of factual claims dramatically reduced their persuasiveness in the 2025 Canadian national and Polish presidential elections, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Hackenburg et al. (2025)</ref> found that instructing an AI to persuade with large quantities of facts and evidence was the most effective strategy on UK political issues.

text.text: However, despite these few examples, future work is needed to map how central evidence-based argumentation is to belief change across contexts.

Our results suggest that many conspiracy believers are substantially more evidenceresponsive than the standard portrait of motivated reasoning, epistemic closure, and self-sealing worldviews implies (Biddlestone et al., 2021; Lewandowsky et al., 2013; Sunstein & Vermeule, 2009).
text.formatted: Our results suggest that many conspiracy believers are substantially more evidenceresponsive than the standard portrait of motivated reasoning, epistemic closure, and self-sealing worldviews implies <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Biddlestone et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lewandowsky et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Sunstein & Vermeule, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Participants low in trust in AI, with highly socially embedded beliefs, or previously familiar with anti-conspiracy arguments showed large belief updates.
Although the effect was directionally smaller for beliefs rated very to extremely important to one's worldview, it was still large (in Study 2, 9.8 vs.
14.7 points relative to Control for less important beliefs; interaction p = .112).

Data from Costello et al. (2024, Study 1) are also consistent with individual variation in the propensity to update: participants higher in actively open-minded thinking (the disposition to revise beliefs according to evidence; Pennycook et al., 2020; Stanovich & Toplak, 2019) showed larger belief revision, though the effect was substantial even at low levels of the trait.
text.formatted: Data from <ref type="bibr">Costello et al. (2024, Study 1</ref>) are also consistent with individual variation in the propensity to update: participants higher in actively open-minded thinking (the disposition to revise beliefs according to evidence; <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Pennycook et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Stanovich & Toplak, 2019)</ref> showed larger belief revision, though the effect was substantial even at low levels of the trait.

text.text: However, since the trait was measured after treatment, the direction of this association is uncertain and requires further research.
Our work has several limitations.
First, participants self-selected into online studies and may not represent the most committed believers.
Nonetheless, they enrolled without knowing that the studies concerned conspiracy beliefs, and relatively few dropped out once they learned this.

Relatedly, the sample skews modestly more female (55% vs. 51% of U.S. adults; U.S. Census Bureau, 2024), substantially more educated (56% vs. 36% of U.S. adults aged 25 and older with a bachelor's degree or higher), and substantially less religious (45% vs.

62% Christian; Pew Research Center, 2025) than population estimates; if the treatment's effect varies with these characteristics, our effect sizes may not generalize without adjustment to a probability sample of U.S. adults.

However, moderation tests showed no reliable and significant differences in effect by demographic characteristics, suggesting that the core finding generalizes at least across the demographic range we observed.

Also, the laboratory isolates participants from social and informational networks that may reinforce such beliefs, although the Baseline treatment remained effective even for the most socially embedded beliefs, which addresses the strongest version of this concern.

Second, the No Facts prompt removes a bundle of co-occurring features -specific facts, source citations, claim-level precision -rather than any one of them cleanly, so "facts" here should be read as a set of correlated properties rather than a surgical ablation; and the claim-level analyses, being observational, carry a weaker causal warrant than the experimental contrasts.

Self-reported prior exposure to counterarguments did not moderate the effect, and halving the length of the AI's responses did not detectably weaken it, consistent with the possibility that what matters is not the volume of facts per se but the right counterevidence.

Future work could test this by measuring familiarity with the AI's arguments and by varying the amount of evidence more finely and its selection, specificity, sourcing, framing, and personalization factorially.
Even so, the overall picture is difficult to square with a strong-form motivated-reasoning account of conspiracy belief.

Given relevant, specific, personalized counterevidence, many firm conspiracy believers update substantially: In Study 2, nearly a quarter (23%) of Baselinetreatment participants who began above the scale midpoint ended below it.

Conspiracy beliefs do not appear to blind all believers to evidence; instead, conspiracies may survive in an epistemic environment where relevant counterevidence and argument, appropriately framed, are rarely delivered.
Generative AI models are remarkably good at addressing this deficit.

text.text: Overview of the Experimental Procedure
text.formatted: Overview of the Experimental Procedure</head>

text.text: Study 1 ran in two waves from the same participant pool under one protocol, apart from two sentences of the No Facts prompt (Samples 1a and 1b; §S6.2).
After giving consent, participants completed a CAPTCHA; those who failed it or opened the survey on a mobile device were screened out ( §S2.1).

They then answered an open-ended writing screener ( §S1.3.3), demographic and political items that included an attention check, and questions about their familiarity with, use of and trust in AI ( §S1.3.5).
Participants were then randomly assigned to a condition (Table S1; a ninth, alternative-model arm in Sample 1a is excluded, §S2.1).
text.formatted: Participants were then randomly assigned to a condition (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>; a ninth, alternative-model arm in Sample 1a is excluded, §S2.1).

text.text: Next, participants described a conspiracy theory they found credible and elaborated on what led them to believe it (wording in §S1.3.4).
GPT-4 (gpt-4-0125-preview, also used for the Study 1 classifier and dialogue) summarized the two answers in one sentence (prompts in §S1.3.1).
Participants rated their confidence that this statement was true (0-100) and said whether the summary was accurate.

In the Belief-First Rating condition the order differed: participants answered the initial conspiracy prompt, rated a statement that was generated from that first response alone (a one-question variant of the summarization prompt, reproduced in §S1.3.1), and only then completed the elaboration prompt, before the dialogue.
The rated statement in Belief-First Rating was therefore shorter (22.2 vs.
32.2 words); participants flagged it as an inaccurate summary no more often than in the six standard-procedure arms (3.6% vs.
5.6%; Fisher's exact p = .42).
In the Abstracted Summary condition, the summarization prompt also told the AI not to mention any specific evidence the participant had given ( §S1.3.1).
In Study 1, GPT-4 then judged whether the answers expressed a conspiracy belief, using the YES/NO prompt validated in Costello et al.
(2024; §S1.3.2); participants judged not to were routed to parallel questions and a parallel dialogue about a non-conspiratorial belief.
Participants with a conspiracy belief then saw condition-specific instructions and had three rounds of chat with GPT-4, whose system prompt differed by condition (Table S1).
text.formatted: Participants with a conspiracy belief then saw condition-specific instructions and had three rounds of chat with GPT-4, whose system prompt differed by condition (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: After the chat they rated the same statement again (0-100).
Those whose rating had fallen were asked what they found persuasive in the AI's comments, and the others why they did not ( §S1.3.4).
Study 2 followed the Study 1 procedure, except as follows.

On the same page as the pretreatment belief rating, before random assignment, participants also answered two measures used as moderators ( §S5): four items on prior exposure to counterarguments against their belief, and one item on whether close others (friends, family) endorse it (social embeddedness; wording in the main text).
The restatement and classifier prompts were gpt-4o variants (classifier wording in §S1.3.2), a second attention check was added ( §S1.3.5), and there were no open-ended persuasion questions.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions, all run with GPT-5.2 (gpt-5.2-2025-12-11).
The Baseline treatment (labeled Full Dialogue in some tables) was the same three-round conversation as in Study 1.
In Single Message, participants read one personalized AI message tailored to the reasons they had given, with no further exchange.
In Control, participants had a conversation of comparable format on one of three unrelated topics, assigned at random: the American medical system, firefighters, or cats versus dogs.
Belief was measured again immediately after the AI interaction in every condition.

Participants were excluded if they (a) failed the attention check (one item in Study 1, two in Study 2; §S1.3.5), (b) failed the writing screener ( §S1.3.3), which ran inside the survey before the experiment and so has no step in Figures S1-S2, (c) did not articulate a conspiracy belief according to the classifier ( §S1.3.2), or (d) rated their pretreatment belief below 50.

text.text: The Bayesian models that organize the main text were not preregistered.

They regress belief reduction (pre -post) on condition (reference: Baseline treatment) and centered pretreatment belief (Gaussian likelihood, fit with brms), with weakly informative priors: Normal(0, 20) on regression coefficients, Normal(0, 30) on the intercept and Student-t(3, 0, 20) on the residual SD.
Bayes factors are two-sided Savage-Dickey density ratios at zero, reported as BF10 or, for null differences between conditions, as BF01 (evidence for the null).
A difference of two coefficients, such as Single Message versus Control in Study 2, has a wider implied prior (Normal(0, 28.3)).
When zero lies several posterior SDs from the mean, the density at zero cannot be estimated reliably, and the Bayes factor is reported as "> 1,000".

text.text: One might expect participants who had already heard many counterarguments to respond less, because they would already know some of what the AI says.
They did not.

The composite records how much counterargument people recall, not its quality: what people meet on their own is usually generic and scattered, whereas the AI's counterevidence is detailed and tailored.
What matters may also be counterevidence that is new to the person, which recalled exposure captures only weakly; the present measures cannot separate these readings.

text.text: Table S19 gives the definitions used in our annotation prompt. Costello et al. (2024) rated all strategies in one GPT-4 Turbo prompt; we rated each strategy in a separate call, with shortened definitions, an added "Uncertain" option and a rating for each of the three AI turns.

(2024)</ref> rated all strategies in one GPT-4 Turbo prompt; we rated each strategy in a separate call, with shortened definitions, an added "Uncertain" option and a rating for each of the three AI turns.

text.text: For each conversation and strategy, GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06, temperature 0) rated the AI's use of the strategy in each round and returned the ratings as JSON.
All 1,401 rated conversations (every Study 1 arm, including participants later excluded from the analytic sample) were coded.
"Uncertain" was returned for 14 of the 22,416 first-round ratings (0.06%).
Only the first-round ratings (the AI's first message) enter the PCA, the prompt contrasts, the GAM and the mediation model.
A simplified excerpt of the prompt follows; in it the AI is the "Debunker" and the participant the "Believer".
"You are an expert annotator analyzing persuasion strategies in conversations on conspiracy theories.
You will see a written conversation between two individuals: a Debunker and a Believer.
The Debunker's role is to convince the Believer that their conspiracy theory is incorrect.
Each conversation has 3 rounds.

Table S19 Definitions of 16 Persuasive Strategies Used to Prompt GPT-4o Strategy Definition Alternative Explanations Provide plausible, evidence-based alternative perspectives or explanations for events attributed to conspiracy theories.
Analogies / Metaphors Use analogies or metaphors to simplify complex information or draw parallels.
Build Rapport Establish a respectful and understanding relationship with the Believer.
Common Ground Identify and build on shared beliefs or values.
Conflicting Evidence Introduce facts that contradict claims made by the conspiracy theory.
Credible Sources Introduce information from reliable sources.
Critical Thinking Encourage the Believer to question the logic and sources behind their beliefs.
Encourage Empathy Help the Believer consider the impact of beliefs on others.
Expert Consensus Emphasize agreement among credible authorities.
Harm Discuss the personal or societal harms of conspiracy beliefs.
Inconsistencies / Fallacies Identify logical inconsistencies or fallacies in arguments.
Maintaining Patience Demonstrate patience in engaging in gradual dialogue.
Offer Resources Provide resources for further learning or alternative perspectives.
Psychological Needs Address emotional aspects or psychological needs related to beliefs.
Socratic Questioning Use a questioning approach to examine beliefs.
Stories / Examples Share stories, anecdotes, or examples.
First-round ratings were scored None = 0, Low = 1, Moderate = 2, High = 3.

text.text: Table S23 Six-Category Claim Taxonomy Category (subtypes) Definition Example claims (assigned subtype) Specific empirical (SE1-SE6) Concrete, checkable claims about events, records, actors, procedures, findings, documents, or physical evidence.
"Operation Northwoods was a 1962 Pentagon proposal involving staged incidents."
(Historical events and documented precedent) / "The Apollo flag had a horizontal rod along the top edge to hold it out."

(Physical / forensic / visual evidence) Inferentiallogical (IL1-IL6) Object-level reasoning about what would follow if the conspiracy were true, what evidence should exist, how coordination would work, or why a mundane alternative is more plausible.
"It would require keeping a secret amongst thousands of people for over 50 years if the moon landing were faked."
(Coordination / leak-risk logic) / "If there were alien craft or bodies, you would expect consistent documentation that survives scrutiny."
(Necessary-evidence-if-true reasoning) Meta-epistemic (ME1-ME3) Claims about how one should evaluate evidence, compare sources, apply standards of proof, or reason under uncertainty.
"Verified evidence of alien life would require evidence that clearly cannot be explained by anything else and can be checked by many independent experts."
(Evidencestandard norm) / "The scientific method involves hypothesis testing, evidence gathering, and peer review."
(Reliability / method guidance) Moral / political evaluation (MP1-MP3) Moral, civic, political, or prudential evaluations about power, justice, abuse, policy risk, empathy, or public consequences.
"In democracies, the electorate is the ultimate check on government."
(Civic / prosocial value) / "If exposed, allowing such an attack would be one of the biggest crimes in US history."
(Moral / justice evaluation) Minimal / nonadjudicative (LI1 -LI5) Definitional, tautological, banal, minimally informative, or merely background statements that do little adjudicative work.
"Logical fallacies are errors in reasoning that weaken arguments."
(Definitional clarification) / "Parkland Hospital is the same hospital where Kennedy and later Oswald were taken."
(Minimal event/background fact) General / underspecified (GU1-GU7) Broad, hedged, contextual, or underspecified claims that are not precise enough to verify as written.
"Most evidence for aliens at Area 51 is anecdotal and hard to verify."
(Absence-of-clear-evidence framing) / "Governments do hide things, mostly for military reasons."

text.text: The grid was ranked by a score that favored 8-12 topics, but those solutions merged distinct themes (e.g., Mandela Effect, Mass Surveillance, Chemtrails) into broad clusters.
We therefore used the 18-topic solution at minPts = 10 (noise fraction = 0.41); the 8-12-topic solutions gave similar topic-level rankings on the topics they kept.
Re-embedding can shift cluster boundaries slightly, so all analyses use the cached cluster assignments distributed with the code ( §S11).
Retained clusters have at least 10 members.
CV = coefficient of variation of retainedcluster sizes; study segregation = how strongly clusters separate Study 1 from Study 2 participants (lower is better).
Solutions with 8-12 retained clusters are ranked first, by noise fraction and then study segregation; ranks 10-15 are omitted (full grid in the replication materials, §S11).

text.text: "You are provided with a list of participant responses regarding why a persuasive conversation with an AI either succeeded or failed in changing their beliefs.
Your role is to annotate each response as an expert coder.

Although you are coding one theme for this task, please keep in mind the definitions of all the following categories: [List of categories and definitions] Today, your focus is on the following theme: [Name and definition] Note: Themes with a '+' in their name (e.g., EVID+, EMPH+) should be coded when the participant praises the AI's attributes.
Themes with a '-' in their name (e.g., LACK-, BIAS-) should be coded when the participant criticizes the AI's persuasive qualities.
In this case, the AI was determined to have [succeed_or_failed] in changing beliefs.
The participant's response was provided in answer to the following question: [posttreatment question].
The response itself will be piped in as the first user response.
Instructions: 1.
Read the participant's response carefully.
Decide if the theme defined above applies.
If it does, output 1; if it does not, output 0.3.
If you are unsure, err on the side of caution and output 0.
That is, AVOID FALSE POSITIVES.
Output your answer strictly in JSON format exactly as follows (do not include any extra text, only 0 or 1): [JSON instructions]."
Table S31 Definitions of the 15 Participant-Account Attributes Attribute (short code) Definition Evidence / Facts / Logic / Counterarguments (EVID+)

The respondent (a) mentions or alludes to concrete data, statistics, facts, and/or (b) mentions logic, rationality, legibility, or appeals to common sense, and/or (c) notes the AI addressed or anticipated their doubts, questions, or alternative views.
Expertise / Credibility / Trustworthiness (EXPT+)

The respondent (a) describes the AI as knowledgeable, authoritative, or expert-like and/or (b) as a reliable, unbiased, or "neutral" source of information and/or (c) values the AI's reliance on trustworthy sources and/or (d) views the AI as having unique or impressive access to what is true by dint of being an AI.
Empathy / Politeness / Respectfulness (EMPH+)

The respondent (a) highlights that the AI was nonjudgmental, supportive, understood their feelings, or validated their viewpoint -even if it disagreed -and/or (b) calls out the AI's polite, kind, or courteous manner and/or (c) mentions feeling calmer, relieved, or emotionally supported by the AI.
Detailed / In-Depth / Novel / Tailored (DETL+)

The respondent (a) praises the AI for being thorough, detailed, or in-depth and/or (b) mentions that the AI introduced new perspectives, angles, or data they hadn't considered and/or (c) that the AI's response was multi-faceted or point-by-point, covering the topic thoroughly and/or (d) that the AI's response was personalized, tailored to their specific questions.

The respondent (a) describes specific mechanisms or details of the conspiracy theory, such as how the building's structure led to collapse, how UFO sightings are often secret aircraft, or forensic details of the JFK case, and/or (b) mentioned a meta-point relevant to conspiracy theories, like that large conspiracies would be impossible to hide since someone would have "spilled the beans".
Privacy (PRIV+)
The respondent felt they could ask the AI questions without fear of judgment or repercussions.
Perceived lack of AI disagreement (LACK-)
The respondent indicates that they already held the belief in question and that the AI merely reaffirmed what they already believed.
Repetition / Regurgitation / Lack of Novelty / Lack of Deep Engagement (DEEP-)

The respondent criticizes the AI for repeating well-known or familiar arguments, offering nothing new beyond what they'd heard before and/or the AI is seen as failing to challenge or engage with the respondent's specific points -merely echoing them rather than providing a substantive counterpoint.
Offensiveness / Anger (ANGR-)
The respondent appears angry or upset about the conversation.
The respondent argues that the AI's response lacked hard data, concrete evidence, or sources to back up its claims.
The respondent perceives that the AI's arguments are skewed toward a particular narrative and fail to engage alternative viewpoints.
Impersonal Tone / Verbosity / Lack of Nuance (MECH-)
The response is critiqued for being too long-winded, mechanical, or overly formal -lacking the human touch or nuance that might otherwise engage the reader.
The respondent expresses skepticism toward the idea that an AI -due to its machine nature, limitations, or potential biases -can be a convincing or trustworthy source.
Off-Topic / Superficial Engagement (OFFT-)
The respondent notes that the AI's responses stray from addressing the core issue or are too general, failing to target the specific points of the debate.
The respondent finds that the AI's arguments lack a personal, emotional, or experiential dimension, making the discussion feel disconnected from real human concerns.
Participants whose belief fell most often said that the AI gave them new facts or evidence and argued logically and clearly.
Some also described its tone as polite, patient, or nonconfrontational, and some valued that it acknowledged their concerns while refuting them or answered their points one by one.
About 5% mentioned the argument that a large conspiracy would be impossible to hide.
Among participants whose belief did not fall, some said they already agreed with the AI, although it had in fact disagreed with them.

Others said it did not engage with their points ("Made oppositional claims without comprehending my points and argument fully"), strayed off topic (mostly in No Facts: "The AI didn't really address my questions, it kind of just reverted back to its message of not questioning the unknown."), repeated itself, or gave no sources ("I wanted their sources.
… I didn't want similar.
I wanted their sources."), often with a charge of bias toward an "official story."
Some rejected AI as a source ("Because I have zero trust in AI, and it's not something we should be messing with.

This technology will kill us all."), and some found it cold, textbook-like, or blind to emotional and lived experience ("They felt a little cold. … it felt like I was reading words from a textbook rather than having a conversation.").

Some positive attributes appear among unchanged-or-increased participants, and some criticisms among belief-reduced participants; they are kept as coded.
Because codes overlap, we count them by participant (11.2% and 15.1%) rather than by summing bars.

Reading these responses, most are mixed or contrary appraisals: praise with a caveat, participants whose belief fell slightly but who deny having been persuaded, and unchanged participants who say the AI was persuasive or report a slider error.
Criticisms became rarer as the belief reduction grew.

The same reading showed recurrent coding errors: CONX+ applied when participants restated their own theory, EVID+ for negated mentions of evidence, LACK-for "I agree with the AI", and EVID-when the evidence said to be lacking is the conspiracy's.
These errors concentrate in the small off-pattern cells.

text.text: To check whether claim composition depended on how true participants' focal conspiracies were, we labeled each focal belief (the AI's one-sentence restatement) with Perplexity Sonar Pro (a web-searching language model).

The prompt asked it to judge the belief's central conspiratorial implication rather than its background premises, and to return a 0-100 veracity score and one of four labels: false or mostly false, mixed or partly true, plausible or mostly true, or too vague to check.
Of the 1,290 Study 1 participants, 70.2% held a false or Both treatments reduced belief relative to Control.

Reduction was larger at higher pretreatment belief (see §S4.5 on regression to the mean) and higher AI trust, and smaller at higher belief importance, more Republican party preference and greater social embeddedness.
Age, religiosity, education and prior exposure to counterarguments showed no independent association.
